text: In the first video you saw what EagleEye can do. Here is how it works, and how it holds up when the whole company logs in at once.
EagleEye is a web app in front, a set of services on AWS in the middle, and the company's data underneath. Every request you are about to see travels this map.
The web app runs on Vercel. Sign-in is handled by Clerk. Everything else, the API, the queue, the workers and the data, lives on AWS.
When someone signs in, Clerk checks who they are and issues a short-lived token. Every request to the API carries it, and the API checks it, and the person's role, every time.
When a document is uploaded, the file goes to secure storage and a job joins the queue, so the upload returns at once.
An ingest worker reads it: the text, the tables, even the charts, which a vision model describes in words. Every passage is turned into a vector and indexed for search.
A question takes the same road. The API places it on the queue and an agent worker picks it up.
First a safety check reads it. Then a planner decides what it needs: a document search, a database query, a notebook analysis, or all of them at once.
Database questions go through a gateway that only allows read-only queries, limited to what the person may see. Analysis code runs in an isolated sandbox with no internet access.
Finally the answer is written from the results, every figure is checked against them, and the answer streams back with its citations.
A malicious request stops at the safety check. A request for data someone isn't allowed to see stops at the gateway. Both are recorded for the administrators.

For a handful of users, one small server is enough. When the whole company arrives, the same services run on a cluster that grows on its own: the more questions waiting in the queue, the more workers it starts.
Let's put that to the test.
